explanations.explanation: Terrified is right, baker. The text says Moab was terrified of the people because they were numerous, and then adds, "Indeed, Moab dreaded the Israelites." (Numbers 22:3) Moab didn't just get nervous, it said it twice. That's a whole nation checking the locks.

I get the thought, but the text never says jealous. It says Moab was terrified, and that Moab dreaded the Israelites. (Numbers 22:3) Jealous is when you want what your neighbor has. This is more like seeing your neighbor's whole crowd pull up and wanting to hide behind the couch.

Nobody in this verse is yawning, friend. Israel is the one that traveled and camped, and Moab is the one with the problem. The text says Moab was terrified and dreaded the Israelites because they were numerous. (Numbers 22:3) Moab wasn't ready for a nap, it was ready to panic.

Pethor by the Euphrates, yes. The text says Balaam is at Pethor, "which is by the Euphrates in the land of his people." (Numbers 22:5) Balak didn't call somebody down the street. He sent messengers out to a man by a famous river, and that tells you how badly Balak wanted him.

Joppa is a real place, but it isn't where this story sends the messengers. The text puts Balaam at Pethor, which is by the Euphrates, in the land of his people. (Numbers 22:5) Joppa is a seaside town in other stories. These messengers were looking for a riverside address.

Bethel is a real place, but it's not on Balak's map this time. The text says Balaam lives at Pethor by the Euphrates, in the land of his people. (Numbers 22:5) The messengers weren't just crossing town. They were headed toward a river.

A curse is what he wants. Balak, king of Moab, says, "So please come now and put a curse on this people, because they are too mighty for me." (Numbers 22:6) He's not asking Balaam to swing a sword. He's asking for words, and he's sure they'll count.

Not quite, friend. Balak doesn't ask Balaam to lead anybody into battle. He asks Balaam to come and put a curse on this people, because they are too mighty for him. (Numbers 22:6) He hopes that after the curse, he may be able to defeat them.

Peace would have been a very different message. Balak is the one who says they are too mighty for him, and he asks Balaam to put a curse on them. (Numbers 22:6) He also hopes to drive them out of the land. A peace treaty wasn't on the menu.

Close, but the text says the opposite. Balak tells Balaam this people is "too mighty for me." (Numbers 22:6) He only says, "Perhaps I may be able to defeat them and drive them out of the land." That's a king hoping for help, and "perhaps" is not a guarantee.

False is right, baker. Balak says the people are "too mighty for me," and then only says, "Perhaps I may be able to defeat them and drive them out of the land." (Numbers 22:6) He's not bragging about his army. He's asking Balaam for backup, and he knows it.

True is right. Balaam says, "Spend the night here, and I will give you the answer that the LORD speaks to me." (Numbers 22:8) Notice he doesn't answer on the spot. He tells the men to wait for the LORD's answer, and the princes stay with him.

It's true, friend. Balaam tells the men, "Spend the night here, and I will give you the answer that the LORD speaks to me." (Numbers 22:8) He doesn't answer on the spot. The princes of Moab stay with him for the night.

Blessed is it, baker. God tells Balaam, "Do not go with them. You are not to curse this people, for they are blessed." (Numbers 22:12) That's the whole reason. You can't curse what God has blessed, and Balak is about to find that out the hard way.

That's a fair guess, but the text doesn't say that. God says Balaam is not to curse this people, "for they are blessed." (Numbers 22:12) Nothing in the verse says they're packing up. Balak wants them gone, but God's reason is that they are blessed.

Armed makes sense with a nation this big, but it isn't what God says. His words are, "You are not to curse this people, for they are blessed." (Numbers 22:12) The reason is a blessing, not weapons. God doesn't mention a single sword here.

True is right. Balaam gets up the next morning and tells Balak's princes, "Go back to your homeland, because the LORD has refused to let me go with you." (Numbers 22:13) He puts it on the LORD, plainly. No hedging, no "let me think about it."

It's true, friend. Balaam says, "Go back to your homeland, because the LORD has refused to let me go with you." (Numbers 22:13) He tells them the real reason. The princes then go back to Balak, and what they report comes next.

Honor him richly, yes. The new princes say, "for I will honor you richly and do whatever you say." (Numbers 22:17) "Whatever you say" is a big promise from a king. Balak went from asking to offering Balaam the keys to the kingdom.

explanations.answer: To give him half of Moab
explanations.explanation: That would be a big offer, but it's not in the text. Balak's promise is, "I will honor you richly and do whatever you say." (Numbers 22:17) He never puts a number or a piece of land on the table. He just promises honor, and that Balaam's word will be followed.

Nice try, but the text doesn't say that. Balak's promise is, "I will honor you richly and do whatever you say." (Numbers 22:17) Notice that the princes are the ones carrying the message. Balak never offers Balaam a title.

Command is right, baker. Balaam says, "If Balak were to give me his house full of silver and gold, I could not do anything small or great to go beyond the command of the LORD my God." (Numbers 22:18) That's a mighty strong answer to a house full of silver and gold. Keep that line in your pocket, because we'll see how it holds up.

Patience would be a fun answer, but it's not what Balaam says. He says he could not do anything small or great "to go beyond the command of the LORD my God." (Numbers 22:18) The line is about obeying the LORD, not about how long Balaam can wait. Even a house full of silver and gold doesn't change that.

Reach sounds good, but Balaam says something else. He says he could not do anything small or great "to go beyond the command of the LORD my God." (Numbers 22:18) It's not about what he can grab. It's about whose command he stays within.

explanations.answer: Go with them but do only what I say
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. God says, "Since these men have come to summon you, get up and go with them, but you must only do what I tell you." (Numbers 22:20) Go, but only with God's words. Hold on to that "but," because it matters a lot in the next scene.

explanations.answer: Send these men home for good
explanations.explanation: That sounds like the first night, friend. Back then God said, "Do not go with them." (Numbers 22:12) This time the word is different: "get up and go with them, but you must only do what I tell you." (Numbers 22:20) Same man, new night, new instructions.

explanations.answer: Stay here and bless Moab instead
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. God tells Balaam, "Since these men have come to summon you, get up and go with them, but you must only do what I tell you." (Numbers 22:20) Nothing in this verse is about blessing Moab. It's about going, and doing only what God tells him.

True is right. The text says, "Then God's anger was kindled because Balaam was going along." (Numbers 22:22) Balaam is on the road with the princes of Moab, and God's anger is on him. We're about to see what the road has waiting.

It's true, friend. Right after Balaam heads out with the princes of Moab, the text says, "Then God's anger was kindled because Balaam was going along." (Numbers 22:22) That's a heavy turn in the story. Things on this road are about to change fast.

A field, yes. The text says, "When the donkey saw the angel of the LORD standing in the road with a drawn sword in his hand, she turned off the path and went into a field." (Numbers 22:23) She sees what Balaam doesn't. And she changes course right away.
She does move, but not that way. The text says she "turned off the path and went into a field." (Numbers 22:23) She doesn't head home. She just gets out of the road, away from the drawn sword.

That would be dramatic, but it isn't in the text. When the donkey sees the angel of the LORD, "she turned off the path and went into a field." (Numbers 22:23) Balaam stays on her. I think he's just confused, because the angel is something only she can see right now.

Foot is right, baker. The text says the donkey "pressed herself against the wall, crushing Balaam's foot against it." (Numbers 22:25) She's squeezed in a narrow passage between two vineyards. Balaam's foot ends up in the middle of it.

Close to the right spot, but it's not a hand. The text says she "pressed herself against the wall, crushing Balaam's foot against it." (Numbers 22:25) With walls on both sides, the passage is tight. His foot is what gets caught.

Almost, friend, but lower down. The text says the donkey "pressed herself against the wall, crushing Balaam's foot against it." (Numbers 22:25) The passage between the two vineyards has walls on either side. His foot is what ends up pinned.

She lies down, baker. The text says, "When the donkey saw the angel of the LORD, she lay down under Balaam." (Numbers 22:27) With no room to turn right or left, she lies right there in the road. Whatever she's doing, she's not walking forward.
She doesn't kick, friend. The text says she "lay down under Balaam." (Numbers 22:27) The place is narrow, with no room to turn to the right or left. She lies down and stays put.

That's a bold idea, but the text shows something else. In that narrow place with no room to turn, the donkey "lay down under Balaam." (Numbers 22:27) She doesn't try to push through. She stops completely.

That's the one. "Then the LORD opened the donkey's mouth, and she said to Balaam, 'What have I done to you that you have beaten me these three times?'" (Numbers 22:28) It's the LORD who does it, not the donkey. And right after that she's the one asking a question.

Nope, the staff stays in one piece. After Balaam beats the donkey a third time, "the LORD opened the donkey's mouth." (Numbers 22:28) Nobody saw this coming. The next thing in the story is a donkey talking.

explanations.answer: He sends a storm on the road
explanations.explanation: No storm here, friend. What happens is that "the LORD opened the donkey's mouth." (Numbers 22:28) The road stays quiet. It's just a donkey, a rider and a voice that wasn't there a minute ago.

explanations.answer: You have made a fool of me
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. Balaam answers her, "You have made a fool of me!" (Numbers 22:29) Look at that. A donkey just started talking and he's already arguing back. I think he's too worked up to be surprised.

explanations.answer: Who taught you how to speak
explanations.explanation: That would be a fair question, but Balaam doesn't ask it. He answers the donkey, "You have made a fool of me!" (Numbers 22:29) He goes straight into the argument. A talking donkey and he keeps right on talking.

Balaam doesn't say that here. His answer is, "You have made a fool of me!" (Numbers 22:29) He's still angry in this moment. The words "I have sinned" come later, after the LORD opens his eyes (Numbers 22:31, 34).

Not quite, friend. The donkey asks, "Am I not the donkey you have ridden all your life until today? Have I ever treated you this way before?" And Balaam answers, "No." (Numbers 22:30) That's a pretty strong reference from a donkey. A whole lifetime of good rides and one strange day.

False is right, baker. The donkey asks, "Have I ever treated you this way before?" and Balaam replies, "No." (Numbers 22:30) She's been his donkey all his life until today. Even Balaam can't argue with her record.

Facedown is right. The text says, "Then the LORD opened Balaam's eyes, and he saw the angel of the LORD standing in the road with a drawn sword in his hand. And Balaam bowed low and fell facedown." (Numbers 22:31) First the donkey's mouth gets opened, and now Balaam's eyes. Once he sees the angel, he goes low.

That's a natural thing to picture, but the text says otherwise. Balaam "bowed low and fell facedown." (Numbers 22:31) He sees the angel of the LORD with the drawn sword, and he goes down in front of him.

He does go down, friend, but the text doesn't say he went silent. It says he "bowed low and fell facedown." (Numbers 22:31) And in the verses right after that, Balaam speaks to the angel (Numbers 22:34).

That's it, baker. The angel says, "If she had not turned away, then by now I would surely have killed you and let her live." (Numbers 22:33) The donkey Balaam kept beating was the one who turned away. Turns out she was doing him a favor the whole time.

explanations.answer: He would have killed the donkey
explanations.explanation: It's the other way around, friend. The angel says, "If she had not turned away, then by now I would surely have killed you and let her live." (Numbers 22:33) The donkey is the one who lives. Balaam is the one who would not have.

explanations.answer: He would have let Balaam pass
explanations.explanation: That's not what the angel says. He says, "If she had not turned away, then by now I would surely have killed you and let her live." (Numbers 22:33) The angel was out there to oppose Balaam, so there was no easy pass. It was the donkey's three turns that mattered.

Sinned is right, baker. Balaam says to the angel of the LORD, "I have sinned, for I did not realize that you were standing in the road to confront me." (Numbers 22:34) A minute ago he was ready to take a sword to his donkey. Now his eyes are open, and the first thing he does is own up.

Obeyed isn't what Balaam says. His first words to the angel of the LORD are, "I have sinned, for I did not realize that you were standing in the road to confront me." (Numbers 22:34) It's a confession, not a report card. He had just been told his way was perverse before the angel (Numbers 22:32).

Not this time, friend. Balaam's first words are, "I have sinned, for I did not realize that you were standing in the road to confront me." (Numbers 22:34) It's a short, honest line. He says it right after he sees the angel with the drawn sword.

Not quite, baker. Balaam does offer to go home, saying, "if this is displeasing in your sight, I will go back home." But the angel answers, "Go with the men, but you are to speak only what I tell you." (Numbers 22:34 to 35) He doesn't send Balaam home. He sends him on with a rule about what to speak.

False is right. Balaam offers to go back home, but the angel of the LORD says, "Go with the men, but you are to speak only what I tell you." (Numbers 22:35) So Balaam goes on with the princes of Balak. Same road, with a clear rule about his words.
